questions.problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $v(x)=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x-({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x))}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 Since ${sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-\frac{1}{2}.$

Let $u={log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}$ and $v={x}^{2}.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot 2x)}{({x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3})}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{x-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{x(1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =(\,1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,)\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating a Quotient of Two Polynomials
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x) = x$ and $v(x) = 9x^2 + 5x,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =18x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\eqalign{
			f'(x) 	& = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}\
				& = \dfrac{\left( 9x^2+5x \right )\cdot 1 -x\cdot \left( 18x+5 \right)}{\left( 9x^2+5x\right)^2}\
				& = \dfrac{\left( 9x^2+5x-18x^2-5x \right)}{\left( 9x^2+5x\right)^2}\
				& = -\dfrac{9x^2}{\left( 9x^2+5x\right)^2}.
		}
$$

                    Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $u=1$ and $v=3x+7.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =0\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\eqalign{
			\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	& = \dfrac{ v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}-u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}}{v^2}\
										& = \dfrac{ \left( 3x+7 \right ) \cdot 0 -1\cdot 3}{\left( 3x+7\right)^2}\
										& = -\dfrac{3}{\left( 3x+7\right)^2}.
		}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We know how to calculate the derivative of the product of two functions, but what if we have a quotient?

For that, we can use the **quotient rule**. The quotient rule is a formula to calculate the derivative of the ratio of two functions like 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac {u(x)}{v(x)}.
$$

The quotient rule for differentiation states that the derivative of the function above is given by

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) \cdot v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}.
$$

For example, suppose that we have the function $f(x)$ given by

$$
f(x)= \dfrac{x}{x^2+1},
$$

and we want to find $f'(x).$ 

Here $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=x^2+1.$  Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug them in the formula, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Justifying the Formula for the Derivative of Tangent
tutorials.problem:
We can now prove that $(\tan x)' = \sec^2{x}$ using the quotient rule. Here's how! 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$
